k: K is fixed from train before looking at val: **K = 110 patches/month** (the current CVSS ≥ 9 CNA rule's train volume) and **K = 305** (the generous fallback rule's volume). That is only 3.4% of val's ~3,262 CVEs a month, and a random pick at K = 110 would catch just 3.5% of exploited CVEs. Note that in val the CNA rule itself grew to 196 patches/month, because 2024-H2 had more (and more critical) CVEs, so following the rule literally already overspends the capacity it was sized for.
own: Followed literally, the current rule (**CVSS ≥ 9, CNA**) patches 196 CVEs/month and catches **33.8%** (23 of 68) of exploited CVEs; precision is only 1.95%. Adding the publication-day phrase check costs **one extra patch per month** (197) and lifts recall to **38.2%**. CVSS ≥ 7 catches 64.7% but needs 1,089 patches/month, 5.6× the budget. The generous fallback rule (41.2% at 313/month) uses hindsight scores and is not available on day 0. With 68 positives, every CI is roughly ±11 points wide.
samek: At the main capacity **K = 110**, ranking by the CNA score catches **23.7%** [13–33] of exploited CVEs, and putting phrase CVEs first raises it to **28.1%** [17–38]: **+4.3 points, better in 94% of bootstrap resamples** (it can only help, since it adds a few certain hits on top of the same ranking). At K = 305 the numbers are 38.3% and 42.7%. Surprisingly, the generous fallback score does **worse** at K = 110 (15.1%): it gives 9.0+ to many more CVEs (313/month), so a 110 budget is spread at random across a big pool of tied 9.8s. **The bar for the models: beat 28.1% at K = 110 and 42.7% at K = 305.**
curve: All rule curves rise slowly. Doubling the budget from 110 to 220 adds only ~12 points, because CVSS mostly separates *severe* from *mild*, not *exploited* from *not exploited*. Even at 1,000 patches/month (31% of all CVEs) the best rule catches only ~65%. The phrase check helps most at small K, where a handful of vendor-confirmed exploits sit at the very top.
miss: At K = 110 the best rule still misses **50 of 68** exploited CVEs. 10 of them have **no CNA CVSS score at all** (MITRE-published CVEs, Google Chrome), so a CVSS rule can never rank them. The rest cluster in vendors with a strong exploitation history (**Microsoft 17**, Palo Alto 4, Google 3, Ivanti 3, Cisco 2) and in edge or remote-access products, often with mid-range CVSS (5.8–7.5). Vendor, product type and the description text carry information that CVSS does not, and that is exactly what the models will use.
split: The **same** preview logistic regression (C = 0.1, balanced weights) at the **same** budget (3.37% of each month's CVEs, the share-of-month equivalent of K = 110, needed because the random evaluation set spans 30 months) catches **38.2%** of exploited CVEs on the honest date split but **59.1%** on a random split. With the flat 110/month budget the date-split figure is 36.8%, the number used in the comparison table: **+21 points of pure illusion**. The reason is visible in the last column: on the random split **51% of the evaluation positives have an exploited 'twin' in training** (same vendor, same month, often the same patch-day bulletin or exploit chain), and the model simply recognises them. On the date split that number is 0%. PR-AUC hides most of the gap (0.108 vs 0.126), which is one more reason we select on recall@K. Even this untuned preview already beats the best rule at K = 110 (36.8% vs 28.1%).
final: On validation, the best day-0 rule a careful team could follow today is **'phrase, then CVSS (CNA)'**: **28.1%** of exploited CVEs at 110 patches/month and **42.7%** at 305. The generous fallback is no better at K = 110 and uses hindsight. An untuned logistic regression on day-0 tabular features already reaches **36.8% / 67.6%**, a first sign that a model can roughly double what CVSS catches at the same capacity. The wide CIs (±10 points) from only 68 positives mean Phase 5 should also lean on grouped CV inside train and the walk-forward folds, not on val alone.
